statement: The Alberta Guide to Hunting Regulations is a summary, not a legal document or a complete listing of the regulations.
Full details of the hunting regulations can be obtained from the nearest Fish and Wildlife office.
A resident may host two non-resident Canadians per year, and one of them must be a family member.
A resident can still host two non-resident Canadians per year, but one must now be a family member.
Non-resident Canadians are not eligible to hold antlered moose partner licences in 2026 because they could not apply for antlered moose draws.
Partner licences for elk special licences were introduced in 2026.
Mandatory harvest reporting for special licences provides data that guides wildlife management decisions.
An unguided non-resident alien game bird hunter on a second seven-day licence in the same year cannot hunt the WMUs chosen on the first licence.
It is the hunter's responsibility to know which WMU they are hunting in and the rules that apply there.
The WMU map in the guide is a small-scale approximation; the legal boundaries are described in the Wildlife Regulation.
County and municipal maps show land ownership, which helps hunters obtain permission for access.
An antlered deer, moose or elk has an antler longer than 10.2 cm (4 in).
An antlered deer, moose or elk has an antler longer than 10.2 cm (4 in); any other is antlerless.
Bait means any food attractant, including minerals and any representation of a food attractant.
A firearm in or on a vehicle, aircraft or boat is loaded if live ammunition is in the breech, chamber or attached magazine; cartridges may be in a detached magazine.
A legal hunting firearm can have any action other than fully automatic.
A resident is a person whose primary residence has been in Alberta for at least six months immediately before the relevant date (plus citizenship or 12 months in Canada).
A WiN (wildlife identification number) is a permanent registration number issued to each hunter and angler.
A weapon includes any device that propels a projectile by explosion, spring, air, gas, string, wire or elastic, so bows and air guns are weapons.
First-time hunters who completed the Alberta conservation and hunter education course must add their certificate number to their WiN profile before buying a licence.
Youth must be at least 10 years old to hunt under any hunting licence in Alberta or to apply for big game draws.
Hunters under 16 need written permission from a parent or guardian to buy hunting licences.
Hunters under 18 hunting with a firearm must be accompanied by a parent, guardian, or an adult 18+ with the parent's written permission.
Youth holding an RCMP Minors Firearm Permit that allows hunting may hunt unsupervised.
Youth under 10 may hunt game birds without a licence when supervised by a licensed adult, and their birds count toward the adult's bag limit.
A youth under 10 hunting migratory birds still needs a free federal Youth Migratory Bird Permit, and the supervising adult needs a migratory bird permit.
A youth who turns 18 during the hunting season may keep hunting with their valid licence.
Hunters must carry their licences (electronic or paper) and applicable paper tags on their person while hunting and produce them for an officer.
To buy a licence that requires tags online, you must already have pre-numbered tags before starting the purchase.
A 10-digit WiN is required to apply for draws and to buy wildlife certificates, licences and replacements.
To hunt big game or game birds, a hunter must hold both a valid wildlife certificate and the applicable hunting licence.
A hunter suspended after a conviction must complete the Alberta conservation and hunter education course, taken after the suspension begins.
A person who does not pay a provincial hunting or fishing fine by the due date is suspended from buying licences and applying for draws until it is paid.
Special licence holders must submit a mandatory harvest report (by Feb 15, or Mar 15 for licences ending after Feb 15); failing to report results in a survey fee before the next certificate or draw.
A hunter host may not accept any payment and must accompany hosted hunters while they hunt big game.
A hunter host must report all hunting by hosted non-resident aliens to Fish and Wildlife by December 31, even if nothing was harvested.
A non-resident alien accompanied by a hunter host may not hunt bighorn sheep, cougar or class 1 pronghorn.
Non-resident (Canadian) and non-resident alien hunters of big game, wolf and coyote must be accompanied by a licensed guide or hunter host, but need no outfitter or guide for game birds.
A designated partner must stay in direct communication (no electronic devices) with the primary special licence holder; the primary carries the tags and tags the kill.
The primary special licence holder may hunt without the partner, but the partner may not hunt without the primary; no tag is issued with a partner licence.
Before buying any licence, every hunter must hold a valid WiN and a wildlife certificate.
Hunting with a bow and arrow requires a bowhunting permit, but hunting with a crossbow does not.
A bowhunting permit is required, in addition to the species licence, to hunt with a bow and arrow.
A resident needs a game bird licence plus a federal migratory game bird hunting permit to hunt waterfowl and sandhill cranes.
To hunt pheasant, a hunter needs both a game bird licence and a pheasant licence.
A game bird licence alone (with WiN and wildlife certificate) covers grouse, partridge, ptarmigan and cormorants; wild turkey needs a draw-only special licence plus a game bird licence.
The resident wildlife certificate costs $35, or $12 for the resident youth/senior certificate.
Licences can be reprinted online at no charge, while a tag replacement requires bringing your licence and ID to a licence issuer.
A resident who killed a sheep (other than a legal class 2 sheep) the previous year may not buy a class 1 sheep licence this year.
The unguided non-resident alien game bird licence is valid in three WMUs for seven continuous days.
Hunters carrying licences electronically in Alberta must use the AlbertaRELM app; tags cannot be carried electronically.
It is unlawful to carry or use another person's licence or tag, or to let someone use yours.
It is unlawful to hunt from an aircraft or drone or to communicate wildlife locations seen during a flight for hunting.
Transporting dead wildlife taken by someone else requires a bill of lading signed by the licence holder.
Prohibited hunting devices include fully automatic firearms, silencers, explosive arrows, live wildlife as decoys, poisons and immobilizing drugs.
Electronic calls are allowed only for snow geese sounds and for crows, magpies, coyote, red fox and wolf.
Pistols and revolvers may not be used for hunting except by a licensed trapper dispatching a trapped animal or air guns under 500 fps.
Hunters must not let the four quarters, loins and neck meat of big game, or game bird breasts, become unfit for consumption.
A loaded firearm (ammunition in breech, chamber or magazine) is prohibited in or on any vehicle, moving or stationary; a detached loaded magazine is allowed.
No one may discharge a weapon, or send a projectile, within 183 m (200 yards) of an occupied building, except the owner/occupant or persons they authorize.
It is unlawful to shoot from or across a provincial highway or a paved, oiled, graded or maintained road; without a ditch or fence the roadway extends 20 feet from the travelled portion.
Hunting or discharging a firearm is prohibited between one-half hour after sunset and one-half hour before sunrise.
A hunter under 18 may hunt with a firearm only with a federal minors permit or when accompanied by a parent/guardian or an authorized adult 18 or older.
Muzzle-loading firearms used for big game must be .44 calibre or greater.
Rimfire ammunition, centrefire bullets under .22 calibre and non-expanding bullets are prohibited for big game.
For big game, an auto-loading firearm may not hold more than five cartridges in the magazine and shotguns of .410 or smaller are prohibited.
It is unlawful to shoot at a big game animal while it is swimming.
A leashed tracking dog may be used for big game only after the animal has been shot at, and must stay leashed at all times.
Hunting a black bear under one year old or a female with such a cub, or a female cougar with a spotted kitten, is unlawful.
A hunter may abandon either the skin or the meat of a black bear or cougar, but not both.
Big game may not be hunted within six hours after getting off an aircraft, except a jet or turboprop.
Game birds must keep evidence of sex and species (one fully feathered wing or the head; head and beard for wild turkey) until home or prepared for cooking.
Migratory game birds may not be hunted with a single bullet, toxic shot, a crossbow or a shotgun larger than 10 gauge.
Shotguns used for game birds may hold no more than three rounds in magazine and chamber combined.
Game birds may not be hunted within 400 m (1/4 mile) of a bait or feeding station.
Hunters must make every effort to immediately retrieve migratory birds they kill or wound and have adequate means to do so.
In most cases, possessing found dead wildlife requires a permit obtained beforehand from Fish and Wildlife.
Hunters may take deer, moose, elk, pronghorn, black bear, coyotes or game birds out of Alberta without an export permit if accompanying the shipment and carrying the licence.
Buying, selling or trading access to land for hunting is unlawful except under a game bird shooting ground licence.
The obligation to pursue and retrieve wounded game does not override the legal requirement to get permission to enter private land.
Hunters should leave gates as found, avoid damaging property or disturbing livestock, and build good relations with landholders.
Permission is always required to enter Indian reserves (band council), Métis settlements (settlement association) and leased agricultural/grazing public land (leaseholder).
In some PLUZs with designated OHV trail networks, hunters must stay on designated trails even when retrieving game.
OHV access is prohibited in most provincial parks and recreation areas and may be limited by counties, PLUZs or temporary restrictions such as fire hazard.
Under the Wildlife Act, a hunter needs permission to enter occupied land plus express consent to hunt or discharge a firearm there.
Occupied lands do not need to be posted with signs to be protected under section 38 of the Wildlife Act.
Under the Petty Trespass Act, entry without permission is prohibited on land that is cultivated, fenced or enclosed, even without notice.
Under the Criminal Code, a person in peaceable possession of property can require a trespasser to leave.
Hunter hosts and designated guides need the landholder's permission to guide on privately held land.
Owners/occupants of private land (and authorized residents) may hunt, but not trap, black bear and coyote on that land without a licence year-round.
For livestock predation, timber wolf may be hunted without a licence on the land and on lands within 8 km, with right of access.
A cougar taken by a landowner without a licence must be registered within one week with skin and skull; dogs may not be used under this authority.
Dogs in provincial parks, wildland parks and recreation areas must be on a leash no longer than 2 m, with limited hunting exemptions.
Hunting is prohibited in ecological reserves and wilderness areas.
Hunting is generally prohibited in provincial parks and provincial recreation areas, with listed exceptions and firearm discharge permits often required.
When not hunting in a park or recreation area with an open season, firearms must be unloaded, encased or dismantled.
Hunting is permitted in wildland provincial parks and Willmore Wilderness Park, but OHVs (and snowmobiles) are not allowed in Willmore.
In road corridor wildlife sanctuaries, hunting is prohibited within 365 m (400 yards) of the road centre-line and firearms must be unloaded and dismantled or encased.
When crossing a road corridor wildlife sanctuary on foot or horseback, the firearm must be unloaded and the person must take a direct route out.
Baiting of all wildlife is not permitted in provincial parks, recreation areas and wildland parks, except for some permitted trappers and guides.
Unless authorized by a conservation officer, it is unlawful to dress, hang or store big game in a provincial park or recreation area.
No one may approach within 800 m (0.5 mile) of certain island seasonal sanctuaries between April 15 and September 15.
In general, only members of a Métis Settlement Association may hunt on a Métis settlement, unless settlement by-laws authorize others.
It is unlawful to discharge a firearm or dress a big game animal within a forest recreation area.
Hunting is prohibited in national parks; firearms are allowed only on through highways and in town sites, unloaded and encased.
Hunting game birds and carrying shotguns are prohibited in game bird sanctuaries except with a special permit.
Bison hunting is prohibited in designated bison protection areas except during the special seasons provided.
Military bases such as CFB Wainwright, CFB Suffield and the Cold Lake Air Weapons Range are closed to hunting except for special seasons.
In the Saskatoon Mountain Primitive Weapons Area, big game may be hunted only with shotguns, muzzleloaders and archery equipment.
OHVs on public land must be registered, insured, display a visible licence plate and have a headlight, tail light, muffler and spark arrestor.
It is unlawful to discharge a weapon at a pronghorn from within 46 m (50 yards) of a vehicle.

In WMUs 400-446 during an open big game season, weapons may not be carried on an OHV from 1 hour before sunrise until noon, except travelling directly to/from an isolated campsite with weapons and ammunition in separate locked containers out of view.
The OHV weapon restriction in WMUs 400-446 applies to all hunters, including bird game hunters.
Recreationists are urged to avoid motorized use of trails marked 'Active Trapline', especially from November through February.
A deer, moose or elk is 'antlered' when it has an antler longer than 10.2 cm (4 in.).
A class 2 bighorn sheep is a female or a male under one year of age.
There is no hunting season for grizzly bear in Alberta; grizzlies have a shoulder hump and a dished face profile.
White-tailed deer flag their large bushy tail when running; mule deer have a black-tipped rope-like tail held down.
A moose calf has a short nose and face and squarish body, and is seldom alone; a cow is larger with a long face and is often alone.
Evidence of sex, species and class must stay attached to the carcass until it reaches a licensed meat facility or is cut and packaged at a residence.
Accepted evidence of sex for deer includes testicles, scrotum or udder, and for deer only, the completely haired tail, attached to the tagged part.
A hunter may debone in the field if the tagged portion of the leg still carries the evidence of sex, species or class.
Moose, elk and deer tags go through the space between bone and tendon of a hind leg just above the hock, never around the antler base.
The tag must be affixed and locked to a big game animal immediately after the kill.
Under a partner licence, the one who kills must immediately inform the other, and the primary licence holder tags the animal on arriving at the carcass.
An authorized bow for big game has a draw weight of at least 16 kg (35 lb) at 71 cm (28 in.).
Big game arrows must be at least 61 cm (24 in.) long, with a non-barbed head cutting at least 7/8 in. wide.
Crossbows for big game need at least 45.4 kg (100 lb) of pull; no bowhunting permit is needed, but they cannot be used in archery-only seasons.
A cougar must be registered at a Fish and Wildlife office within five business days, with skull and skin and evidence of sex attached.
Compulsory registration gives sex ratios, age structure, dates and locations used to set future harvest goals.
Male sheep must be registered within 14 days after the season closes or 30 days after the kill, whichever comes first.
It is unlawful to hunt wildlife or discharge a firearm from one-half hour after sunset to one-half hour before sunrise.
Sunrise and sunset times apply to the specific location and specific day of the hunt.
It is 7:00 p.m. and sunset was at 6:40 p.m.: firing is still legal until 7:10 p.m.
Archery-only seasons allow only bow and arrow; general seasons allow a firearm, crossbow or bow.
A crossbow may not be used during an archery-only season.
In the season tables, a small black box beside a season means a special licence is required.
Hunters, including bowhunters, need a firearms discharge permit to hunt in WMU 936 (Cooking Lake-Blackfoot).
Hunters must ensure that discharging their weapon is not prohibited by county or municipal by-laws.
Dogs are prohibited for cougar in the fall season (residents only) and allowed in the winter season.
Before hunting cougar in winter, hunters must call the cougar hotline to confirm the WMU is still open, because quotas can close it.
Every cougar harvest must be reported by email or text within 24 hours of the kill.
Cougar may be hunted with mouth or hand-operated calls; electronic calls and bait are prohibited.
It is unlawful to hunt a spotted cougar kitten or a female accompanied by one, or a black bear under one year or a female with a cub under one year.
It is unlawful to let a black bear or cougar skin be wasted unless the edible meat is recovered.
Bear bait is prohibited within 1.6 km (1 mi.) of an occupied dwelling unless written authorization is obtained from all dwellings within that distance.
Each bear bait site needs a sign with the owner's name and phone or WiN, warning signs around it, is limited to the season plus two weeks before, and only meat in November.
Bear and cougar meat should be thoroughly cooked to prevent trichinosis, a parasitic infection.
A resident may hunt (but not trap) timber wolf without a licence from the opening of any big game season in a WMU until the end of May (or June 15 where spring bear runs that late).
Coyotes may be hunted year-round on private land and White Area public land with right of access, by holders of a wildlife certificate.
On public land, bait for wolves or coyotes is allowed only from December 1 to March 31 or during a black bear season where bear baiting is permitted.
Porcupine, rabbit, hare, raccoon and woodchuck may be hunted (not trapped) without a licence throughout the province all year.
A resident may hunt red fox without a licence all year on private land to which they have the right of access.
Double-crested cormorants are game birds hunted in duck season with a game bird licence; flesh may be wasted but dead birds must be recovered and disposed of.
Federal regulations prohibit lead shot and crossbows for hunting waterfowl.
Single projectiles (.22 rimfire, centrefire rifle) are illegal for migratory game birds but legal for upland game birds and wild turkey.
Falconers must hold the same hunting licences as firearm hunters; bowhunters of game birds need a bowhunting permit in addition.
Whooping cranes (white body, black wing tips, 7-ft wingspan) are endangered and protected; sandhill cranes are grey or brown.
Sage grouse are endangered and protected in Alberta.
All birds are protected except listed species such as starlings, crows, pigeons, house sparrows, magpies and blackbirds, and birds with an open season.
Swans, often seen in small low-flying flocks in late fall, must not be shot.
Youth under 10 need no provincial game bird licence but must be supervised by a licensed adult, and their birds count in the adult's limit.
Youth under 18 may get a free migratory game bird permit; an accompanying permitted adult may supervise up to two youth.
Male wild turkeys have a beard, gobble, have bright red/blue heads, a wattle, caruncles and a snood.
The daily limit is 8 ducks (each) and 8 Canada/white-fronted geese combined.
Anyone who kills or finds a dead animal fitted with a tracking device must report and return the device to Fish and Wildlife Enforcement Services.
Marked animals that may have received drugs carry a tag advising not to eat the meat before contacting Fish and Wildlife.
Waterfowl leg bands recovered in North America can be reported by phone or on the internet (reportband.gov).
CWD is a fatal prion disease of cervids, mainly mule deer in Alberta; not known to infect humans, but eating animals with prion disease is advised against.
Heads of deer from designated WMUs must be submitted for CWD testing within 30 days; antlers and skull plate may be removed first.
Leave the carcass remains at the kill site; if transported, remove usable meat then burn, bury or landfill the remains.
A bill of lading is used when transporting wildlife taken by another hunter.
When drawn for a special licence, draw priority resets to zero, the draw cannot be cancelled, and you may be unable to buy a general licence for that species.
